title: America’s first satellite found Earth’s radiation belts when its counter went quiet

cover.alt: Black-and-white newsreel still: a slender white rocket stands floodlit on its launch pad at night.

body: **Explorer 1** lifted off from Cape Canaveral at 10:48 p.m. Eastern time on 31 January 1958, four months after the Soviet Sputnik 1. It weighed just 13.97 kg and carried a Geiger counter designed under James Van Allen at the University of Iowa. On low passes the counter registered the expected rate of cosmic rays, but above about 2,000 km over South America it showed zero. The counter was not finding nothing: it was **saturated**, swamped by radiation trapped in belts around Earth that now bear his name.

slides.alt: Black-and-white newsreel at night: a floodlit rocket on the pad, its service arm swinging away, then a burst of flame and billowing smoke as it lifts off; a close-up tracks along the climbing rocket to its exhaust.
slides.caption: Newsreel of the night launch, January 1958: the Juno I rocket, a modified Jupiter-C, lifts off from Cape Canaveral in a burst of flame and smoke.

slides.prompt: Explorer 1 was meant to spin steadily about its long axis, like a bullet. What did it do instead?
slides.answer: It wobbled, then spun about another axis
slides.detail: It began to precess, because flexible parts slowly dissipated its spin energy, and it settled into spinning about its axis of greatest inertia.

slides.heading: How long Explorer 1 kept going
slides.note: It made more than 58,400 orbits before re-entering over the Pacific on 31 March 1970.

slides.question: Which later satellite confirmed the radiation belts by carrying a tape recorder?
slides.explanation: Explorer 3 carried a tape recorder, and its data confirmed that the silence meant a counter overwhelmed by trapped radiation.
